name: Oscan
confidence_why: Thurneysen 1909, Wallace 2008 and Nishimura 2014 agree that Oscan kept stress on the initial syllable into the historical period, arguing from the fact that long vowels are written double only in first syllables, and the lone dissent, von Planta 1892's guess at a Latin-type penultimate accent, rested on evidence he himself called sparse and was answered by Thurneysen 1909. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Wallace 2008 2008.

catalog_quote: [Wallace 2008 sec. 3.5, p.106:] Very little is known about the word accent of any Sabellian language. ... In all Sabellian languages short vowels were lost before word-final ∗s . Short vowels in open medial syllables were also syncopated before the historic period. This vocalic instability suggests that Sabellian had a stress accent which was positioned on the initial syllable of words. The fact that vowel length is indicated only in initial/radical syllables in both Oscan and Umbrian (with rare exceptions) suggests that word-initial/radical accent was still in place during the historical period (Meiser 1986:150; for Oscan antepenultimate accent, see Schmid 1954). [Nishimura 2014 p.185, on Oscan:] the long-vowel notation, that is, the gemination of vowels, appears mostly in initial syllables: e.g. fíísnú ‘ fanum, temple’ ... trííbarak[avúm], tríbarakavúm ‘aedificare, build’ ... audit.reasoning: All three quotations in the record (Wallace 2008:106, Nishimura 2014:185-186, Buck 1904 sec.165) are verbatim in the text files we hold at the stated locators. The classification 'fixed initial (weight-blind), unreviewed/hedged' matches the modern consensus for an extinct epigraphic language where only philological inference is possible: Wallace 2008 (handbook sketch) states it with the appropriate hedge, Nishimura 2014 (dedicated accent article, open access, held) argues it at length, and the primary orthographic argument, Thurneysen 1908 (Glotta 1:240-242), was downloaded now from archive.org and confirms initial word accent 'zu der Zeit, aus der die Inschriften stammen'. Von Planta 1892 sec. 257 (downloaded now, archive.org) concludes the opposite (Latin-type accent in historical Osco-Umbrian), but this is exactly the older minority view the record already lists under the secondary-stress rule and that later work

sources.citation: Zair, Nicholas. 2016. Vowel weakening in the Sabellic languages as language contact. Indogermanische Forschungen (volume, issue and pages not given in the packet or in the open accepted-manuscript copy; not looked up). doi:10.1515/if-2016-0016
sources.quote: All the possible instances of weakening of vowels in Oscan take place in non-initial and non-final open syllables next to a labial. [...] The restriction to non-initial syllables is shared with developments such as syncope and vowel-shortening discussed in Section 3. A plausible explanation of the weakening seen in Oscan is reduction of duration of vowels in unstressed syllables. Since higher vowels tend to have shorter variation, this is liable to lead to raising [...]. Apparently, the lack of stress did not affect the realisations of the vowels enough to be reflected in writing, except when there was the further conditioning factor of lip-rounding
sources.locator: accepted manuscript, p. 7; also p. 3 ('shortening of long vowels in non-initial (i.e. unstressed) syllables took place in both Oscan and Umbrian') and p. 15 ('…
sources.note: Argues that unstressed-vowel weakening in Oscan, Umbrian and Paelignian arose separately in each language as the long-term result of a generalised initial stress accent spreading through contact among Latin, Sabellic and Etruscan.

sources.citation: Thurneysen, Rudolf. 1909 [dated 1908]. Italisches. 1. Die Betonung des Oskischen. Glotta 1: 240-242.
sources.quote: Double-writing of originally simple long vowels occurs in ~70 examples in first syllables (v. Planta I 56) but is rare/uncertain elsewhere; final and medial syllables show none (sole exception tristaamentud, explained as a stonecutter's lapse). 'Die Tatsache, dass nur in der ersten Silbe Vokale doppelt geschrieben werden ... ist daraus zu schliessen, dass die erste Silbe ... Traegerin des Wortakzents war, nicht nur in einer vorhistorischen Periode, sondern zu der Zeit, aus der die Inschriften stammen.'

sources.citation: von Planta, Robert. 1892. Grammatik der oskisch-umbrischen Dialekte. Bd. I: Einleitung und Lautlehre. Strassburg: Truebner. Sec. 257 'Betonung', pp. 589-596.
sources.quote: Accepts Proto-Italic initial accent for prehistoric Osco-Umbrian (p.592 'kaum zu bezweifeln'), but on the strength of geminate simplification (upsannam vs eehiianasum, aamanaffed), Puemune, zicolo- etc. concludes (p.596) 'entschieden wahrscheinlich ... dass im Osk.-Umbrischen in historischer Zeit die juengere lateinische Betonung herrschte' (Latin-type penultimate law in the historical period). This is the older competing analysis already named in the record's srule; refuted by Thurneysen 1908, Benediktsson 1960, Meiser 1986, Nishimura 2014.
